docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Managing Kubernetes clusters at scale often leads to underutilized resources—especially in development, staging, and CI/CD environments that run 24/7 but are only actively used during business hours. This results in unnecessary cloud spend and inefficient resource utilization.

The Hibernation Operator solves this by enabling automated, policy-driven hibernation of workloads. It safely scales down Deployments and StatefulSets to zero during off-hours and restores them to their original state when needed—helping teams reduce costs without sacrificing developer experience.

With the Hibernation Operator, you can:

  • Schedule hibernation using standard cron expressions for sleep and wake times.
  • Target workloads across multiple namespaces using explicit lists or dynamic label selectors.
  • Work with ArgoCD: a deny sync window on the named AppProjects stops ArgoCD from scaling hibernated workloads back up.
  • Empower platform teams with cluster-wide policies via ClusterResourceSupervisor.
  • Enable self-service for application teams using namespace-scoped ResourceSupervisor.
  • Preserve state reliably: Original replica counts are stored in the CR’s status for accurate restoration—even after operator restarts.
  • Integrate seamlessly with existing Kubernetes and ArgoCD workflows, using only native Kubernetes resources.

The Hibernation Operator is lightweight, secure, and built for real-world Kubernetes environments—whether you're running on OpenShift, EKS, AKS, GKE, or vanilla Kubernetes.

docs.text: Refer to the installation guide to deploy the Hibernation Operator in your cluster via Helm or Operator Lifecycle Manager (OLM).

docs.title: v0.1.104
docs.text: September 16, 2026

docs.title: Breaking Changes
docs.text: • ResourceSupervisor now records hibernated replica counts in status.sleepingNamespaces instead of the hibernation.stakater.com/original-replicas annotation on each workload, so GitOps controllers no longer report drift on hibernated workloads. Upgrading requires no action, as the first wake after upgrade restores anything still carrying the old annotation.

docs.title: Bug Fixes
docs.text:
• Fixed StatefulSets never being woken, which also discarded the only record of their original replica count.
  • Fixed a Deployment and a StatefulSet sharing a name colliding, so that only one of them was ever woken.
  • Fixed ResourceSupervisor waking workloads it never put to sleep, and restoring unannotated workloads to a single replica.
  • Fixed a failed wake being reported as success, so the affected workloads were never retried.
  • Fixed deletion removing the finalizer even when the pre-delete wake failed, leaving namespaces asleep with nothing left to retry.
  • Fixed supervisors that reference only ArgoCD applications being rejected by the validating webhook.
  • Fixed an invalid sleep schedule being accepted when no wake schedule was set, after which the supervisor stopped reconciling.
  • Fixed a failed namespace lookup waking every sleeping namespace.
  • Fixed transient errors permanently freezing a supervisor until the operator restarted.
  • Fixed workloads rescaled between sleep passes being woken at a stale replica count.

docs.title: Changes to behavior
docs.text:
• Logging now defaults to production mode (JSON, Info level) instead of debug console output. Pass -zap-devel for the previous behavior.
  • The pprof endpoint no longer listens by default. Pass --pprof-bind-address to enable it.

docs.title: Finding why a sleep or wake failed
docs.text:
When status.currentStatus is error, the reason is on the resource itself, no operator logs needed. The Ready and Reason columns show it for every supervisor at a glance:

kubectl get clusterresourcesupervisors
kubectl get resourcesupervisors -A

For the full message, read the conditions:

kubectl get clusterresourcesupervisor <name> -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions}'
kubectl get resourcesupervisor <name> -n <namespace> -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions}'

The Ready condition carries one of these reasons: True when the workloads are in the state the schedule asks for, False when they are not:

Reason Meaning Reconciled The last sleep or wake succeeded (True) Scheduled The resource is new and nothing is due yet (True) InvalidSleepSchedule sleepSchedule is not a valid cron. The operator stops acting on the resource until it is fixed InvalidWakeSchedule wakeSchedule is not a valid cron. Same as above SleepFailed At least one workload could not be scaled down. The operator retries automatically WakeFailed At least one workload could not be restored. The operator retries automatically NamespacesUnresolved The governed namespaces could not be listed

The condition message carries the underlying error. After a failed wake, each application still asleep also carries its own errorMessage:

status:
  currentStatus: error
  conditions:
    - type: Ready
      status: "False"
      reason: WakeFailed
      message: 'namespace team-a, application web: deployments.apps "web" is forbidden: ...'
  sleepingNamespaces:
    - Namespace: team-a
      status: error
      sleepingApplications:
        - name: web
          kind: Deployment
          replicas: 3
          status: error
          errorMessage: 'deployments.apps "web" is forbidden: ...'

The next sleep clears the errorMessage fields.

docs.title: Workloads stay at zero after a wake
docs.text:
Check the resource's Events for a LedgerLost Warning. The replica counts live only in status.sleepingNamespaces, so if the status was lost the operator has nothing to restore from and leaves the workloads at zero rather than guessing. Scale them back by hand.

A wake only restores workloads the operator slept. A workload that was already at zero when the sleep ran, or was created while the namespace slept, is left alone.

docs.title: Schedules fire at the wrong time
docs.text: Both cron schedules are evaluated in UTC, never in the cluster's or the browser's timezone. sleepSchedule: "0 18 * * *" sleeps at 18:00 UTC.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: The Hibernation Operator scales Deployments and StatefulSets down to zero on a schedule and restores them afterwards, so that environments needed only during working hours stop consuming compute for the rest of the time. It manages two custom resources: the ResourceSupervisor, which a namespace owner creates to hibernate their own namespace, and the ClusterResourceSupervisor, which a platform team uses to hibernate a group of namespaces.

docs.title: Components
docs.text: Deployment Description hibernation-operator-controller-manager Hibernates and restores workloads according to the schedule of each resource, and reports the outcome in its status. hibernation-operator-webhook Validates both resources when they are created or updated.

docs.title: At the sleep time
docs.text: Every Deployment and StatefulSet with a non-zero replica count in the governed namespaces is scaled to zero. Its replica count is recorded in the status of the resource first, so that it can be restored later. Workloads already at zero are left as they are.

docs.title: At the wake time
docs.text: Each workload recorded in the status is restored to its recorded replica count. Workloads that the operator did not hibernate are not modified.

docs.title: When a resource is deleted
docs.text: The workloads of the resource are restored before the deletion completes, and any ArgoCD sync windows it applied are removed. If a restoration fails, the resource is retained until it succeeds.

docs.title: When a namespace is excluded or leaves the selection
docs.text: Namespaces annotated hibernation.stakater.com/exclude: "true", and the namespace in which the operator runs, are never hibernated. When a namespace becomes excluded or is no longer selected, the workloads hibernated there are restored at the next scheduled sleep or wake. Such namespaces are listed in status.ignoreNamespaces.

docs.title: When the operator restarts
docs.text: The schedule is evaluated against the current time rather than against a running timer, and the recorded replica counts are stored in the Kubernetes API. A restarted operator therefore continues where it left off.

docs.title: ArgoCD
docs.text:
ArgoCD treats a workload scaled to zero as drift from Git and scales it back up, which would undo hibernation. When spec.argocd is set on a ClusterResourceSupervisor, the operator applies a deny sync window to the specified AppProjects for the duration of the sleep period.

Note

This is the operator's only interaction with ArgoCD. AppProjects do not determine which namespaces are hibernated; these are always selected through spec.namespaces.

docs.title: Admission validation
docs.text:
The webhook rejects a resource when:

  • A cron expression in spec.schedule cannot be parsed.
  • sleepSchedule and wakeSchedule are identical.
  • wakeSchedule is set without sleepSchedule.
  • A ClusterResourceSupervisor lists the same namespace twice, or selects a namespace already selected by another ClusterResourceSupervisor.

An empty schedule is valid and hibernates the workloads immediately and indefinitely. The webhook does not prevent a namespace from being governed by both a ClusterResourceSupervisor and its own ResourceSupervisor, so such overlaps must be avoided by convention.

The metrics endpoint is described in Metrics.

docs.title: ClusterResourceSupervisor
docs.text:
A ClusterResourceSupervisor applies one hibernation schedule to a group of namespaces. It is cluster-scoped and intended for platform teams parking development, test, or preview environments at scale. For a single namespace managed by the team that owns it, use a ResourceSupervisor.

As with the namespace-scoped resource, only Deployments and StatefulSets are affected.

For the complete field listing, see the API Reference.

docs.title: Selecting namespaces
docs.text:
Namespaces come from spec.namespaces, by explicit name, by label selector, or both. The results are combined, so a namespace selected either way is hibernated.

apiVersion: hibernation.stakater.com/v1beta1
kind: ClusterResourceSupervisor
metadata:
  name: dev-environments-hibernation
spec:
  namespaces:
    names:
      - legacy-staging
    labelSelector:
      matchLabels:
        env: dev
  schedule:
    sleepSchedule: "0 18 * * 1-5"
    wakeSchedule: "0 8 * * 1-5"

labelSelector is a standard Kubernetes label selector, so matchLabels and matchExpressions both work and are combined with AND. It is re-evaluated at each scheduled sleep or wake, so namespaces created later are picked up without editing the resource.

Warning

An empty labelSelector: {} matches no namespaces, not all of them, and a ClusterResourceSupervisor with no spec.namespaces at all hibernates nothing. To cover a broad set, apply a label the target namespaces share and select on that.

docs.title: Scheduling
docs.text:
spec.schedule behaves as it does for ResourceSupervisor: two five-field cron expressions evaluated in UTC. Setting both cycles the workloads, and omitting wakeSchedule sleeps them at the next sleep time and leaves them asleep.

spec:
  schedule:
    sleepSchedule: "0 22 * * *"
    wakeSchedule: "0 6 * * *"

docs.title: Exclusions
docs.text:
Two filters run after selection, and a namespace caught by either is reported in status.ignoreNamespaces rather than hibernated:

  • The namespace is annotated hibernation.stakater.com/exclude: "true".
  • The namespace is the one the operator itself runs in.

Anything the supervisor already slept in a namespace that becomes excluded is woken. The annotation is how an individual team opts out of a platform-wide policy without needing the selector changed.

docs.title: Overlap between supervisors
docs.text:
The admission webhook rejects a ClusterResourceSupervisor that claims a namespace already claimed by another one, and also rejects duplicate names within a single resource. Two cluster-scoped supervisors therefore cannot fight over the same namespace.

Warning

That check does not extend to ResourceSupervisor. A namespace can hold its own ResourceSupervisor while also being selected here, and both controllers will then act on the same workloads on their own schedules. Exclude the namespace with the annotation if it should manage itself.

docs.title: ArgoCD sync windows
docs.text:
Workloads managed by ArgoCD present a problem: scaling them to zero is drift from Git, and ArgoCD will scale them back up. The spec.argocd field addresses this by writing a deny sync window onto the AppProjects you name, covering the sleep schedule and its computed duration.

spec:
  namespaces:
    labelSelector:
      matchLabels:
        team: frontend
  argocd:
    namespace: argocd
    appProjects:
      - frontend-team
  schedule:
    sleepSchedule: "0 22 * * *"
    wakeSchedule: "0 6 * * *"

Warning

spec.argocd does not select namespaces. It suppresses syncing for the AppProjects listed, nothing more, and the namespaces to hibernate still come entirely from spec.namespaces. A resource with argocd but no namespaces writes sync windows and hibernates nothing.

Two further constraints:

  • The operator replaces spec.syncWindows on each named AppProject rather than appending, so any sync windows maintained there by other means are overwritten.
  • The ArgoCD AppProject CRD must be present. If it is absent the operator logs that and continues hibernating without touching ArgoCD.

docs.title: Status
docs.text:
Field Shows currentStatus running, sleeping, or error watchedNamespaces Namespaces currently being managed ignoreNamespaces Selected namespaces filtered out by the exclusions above sleepingNamespaces Per-namespace detail of scaled-down workloads and their original replica counts. After a failed wake, each application still asleep carries an errorMessage nextReconcileTime Next scheduled sleep or wake conditions Ready, True after a successful sleep or wake and False with the reason after a failed one 
kubectl get clusterresourcesupervisor dev-environments-hibernation -o jsonpath='{.status}'

When a namespace you expected is missing from watchedNamespaces, ignoreNamespaces is the first place to look. When currentStatus is error, read the Ready condition, see Troubleshooting.

The replica counts in sleepingNamespaces are the only record of them. If the status is lost the workloads stay at zero and the operator emits a LedgerLost Warning Event rather than guessing.

docs.title: Choosing between the two
docs.text: Use a ResourceSupervisor when a namespace should decide its own hibernation and the team owning it holds only namespace-level permissions. Use a ClusterResourceSupervisor when a platform team sets the policy across many namespaces, when the set is defined by labels and changes over time, or when ArgoCD sync windows need suppressing during sleep.

docs.title: ResourceSupervisor
docs.text:
A ResourceSupervisor hibernates the workloads in the namespace it lives in. It is namespace-scoped, so a team that owns a namespace can park its own workloads outside working hours without needing cluster-wide permissions. To cover a group of namespaces from one place, use a ClusterResourceSupervisor.

Only Deployments and StatefulSets are affected. Everything else in the namespace is left running.

For the complete field listing, see the API Reference.

docs.title: Scheduling modes
docs.text:
The spec.schedule block accepts two cron expressions, and which of them you set determines the behavior.

sleepSchedule wakeSchedule Behavior Set Set Workloads cycle between the two times Set Omitted Workloads sleep at the next sleep time and stay asleep Omitted Omitted Workloads sleep immediately and stay asleep

Both expressions use standard five-field Unix cron syntax (minute hour day month weekday) and are evaluated in UTC, not the cluster's local timezone.

docs.title: Recurring hibernation
docs.text:
Setting both schedules is the common case, parking an environment overnight and bringing it back in the morning.

apiVersion: hibernation.stakater.com/v1beta1
kind: ResourceSupervisor
metadata:
  name: nightly-hibernation
  namespace: my-app-staging
spec:
  schedule:
    sleepSchedule: "0 20 * * *"   # Sleep daily at 20:00 UTC
    wakeSchedule: "0 8 * * *"     # Wake daily at 08:00 UTC

docs.title: Sleep with no scheduled wake
docs.text:
Omitting wakeSchedule sleeps the workloads at the next sleep time and leaves them there. Workloads are hibernated again at each subsequent sleep time, so workloads added to the namespace later are hibernated too rather than being left running.

spec:
  schedule:
    sleepSchedule: "0 12 * * *"   # Sleep at the next 12:00 UTC, no wake

To bring the workloads back, add a wakeSchedule or delete the resource.

docs.title: Immediate sleep
docs.text:
An empty schedule sleeps the workloads as soon as the resource is created, and hibernates any new workloads within the hour. This suits ephemeral environments such as CI preview namespaces, where the namespace should be parked from the moment it exists.

apiVersion: hibernation.stakater.com/v1beta1
kind: ResourceSupervisor
metadata:
  name: sleep-now
  namespace: ci-preview-pr123
spec:
  schedule: {}

Note

Setting wakeSchedule without sleepSchedule is not supported, and the resource is rejected.

docs.title: Replica counts and restoration
docs.text:
Before scaling a workload down, the operator records its replica count in status.sleepingNamespaces on the ResourceSupervisor, and a wake restores exactly that count. A wake is restore only: a workload the operator never slept is left alone, and no count is ever guessed.

Workloads already at zero replicas are skipped, so they are not later "restored" to zero-with-a-record they never had.

Warning

The status is the only record of the counts. If it is lost, the workloads stay at zero and the operator emits a LedgerLost Warning Event instead of inventing a count. Scale them back by hand.

Versions before v0.1.104 stored the count in the annotation hibernation.stakater.com/original-replicas on each workload, and woke anything without it to 1 replica. The annotation is still read on wake, so workloads slept by an older version come back at their recorded count, but nothing writes it anymore.

Deleting the ResourceSupervisor wakes its workloads first. The resource is retained until the restore succeeds, and a failed wake is retried, which makes deletion the straightforward way to cancel hibernation.

docs.title: Exclusions
docs.text: A namespace annotated hibernation.stakater.com/exclude: "true" is never hibernated, even if a ResourceSupervisor exists in it, and anything already asleep there is woken. The operator's own namespace is excluded the same way. This gives platform teams a way to protect a namespace regardless of what is created inside it.

docs.title: Status
docs.text:
status.currentStatus reports running, sleeping, or error, and status.nextReconcileTime gives the next time the operator will act. The Ready condition in status.conditions says whether the last sleep or wake succeeded, and if not why. See Troubleshooting for its reasons.

kubectl get resourcesupervisor nightly-hibernation -n my-app-staging -o jsonpath='{.status}'

docs.title: Differences from ClusterResourceSupervisor
docs.text:
ResourceSupervisor has no namespaces field and cannot target anything beyond its own namespace, and no argocd field, so it cannot suppress ArgoCD syncing during sleep. If the namespace's workloads are managed by ArgoCD, ArgoCD will see the scaled-down state as drift and may restore it. Use a ClusterResourceSupervisor where that matters.

Warning

Nothing prevents a ClusterResourceSupervisor from also selecting a namespace that already has a ResourceSupervisor. The admission webhook rejects overlap between two ClusterResourceSupervisor resources, but it does not check for this case, and the two controllers will then act on the same workloads independently. Avoid the overlap, or exclude the namespace with the annotation above.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text: Get the Hibernation Operator running and put your first workload on a sleep schedule in a few minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A Kubernetes cluster (v1.24+) with kubectl access
  • Helm CLI
  • cert-manager, which the Helm chart requires for its webhook and metrics certificates

For OpenShift OperatorHub and detailed options, see Installation.

docs.title: 1. Install the operator
docs.text:
helm install hibernation-operator \
  oci://ghcr.io/stakater/public/charts/hibernation-operator \
  --namespace hibernation-operator-system \
  --create-namespace

Wait for the pods to become ready:

kubectl get pods -n hibernation-operator-system --watch

docs.title: 2. Create your first schedule
docs.text:
Create a namespace-scoped ResourceSupervisor that scales the workloads in a namespace down at night and back up in the morning (UTC):

# my-first-schedule.yaml
apiVersion: hibernation.stakater.com/v1beta1
kind: ResourceSupervisor
metadata:
  name: nightly-hibernation
  namespace: my-app-staging   # must match the target namespace
spec:
  schedule:
    sleepSchedule: "0 20 * * *"   # sleep daily at 20:00 UTC
    wakeSchedule: "0 8 * * *"     # wake daily at 08:00 UTC

Apply it:

kubectl apply -f my-first-schedule.yaml

docs.title: 3. Verify
docs.text:
kubectl get resourcesupervisor nightly-hibernation -n my-app-staging \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.currentStatus}'

The currentStatus field reports running, sleeping, or error.

docs.title: Uninstalling
docs.text:
The custom resources must be deleted before the operator itself is removed. Deleting a ResourceSupervisor or ClusterResourceSupervisor restores every workload it put to sleep and, for a ClusterResourceSupervisor, removes the ArgoCD sync windows it applied. That work is done by the operator, so if the operator is removed first, the deletion of the resources does not complete and the hibernated workloads remain at zero replicas.

Uninstall in the following order.

docs.title: 1. Delete the custom resources
docs.text:
While the operator is still running, delete every supervisor:

kubectl delete clusterresourcesupervisors.hibernation.stakater.com --all
kubectl delete resourcesupervisors.hibernation.stakater.com --all --all-namespaces

Each deletion completes once the operator has restored the workloads of that resource. Confirm that none remain before continuing:

kubectl get clusterresourcesupervisors.hibernation.stakater.com
kubectl get resourcesupervisors.hibernation.stakater.com --all-namespaces

If a deletion does not complete, inspect the events on the resource with kubectl describe. A failed restoration is reported there as a WakeFailed event, and the resource is retained until the restoration succeeds.

docs.title: Helm
docs.text:
helm uninstall hibernation-operator --namespace hibernation-operator-system

This removes the operator deployments, RBAC resources and services. Helm does not remove the CRDs, because the chart installs them from its crds/ directory.

docs.title: OpenShift (OLM)
docs.text:
In the OpenShift web console:

  1. Navigate to Operators → Installed Operators and select the hibernation-operator-system project.
  2. Open the actions menu for Hibernation Operator and select Uninstall Operator.
  3. Confirm the removal.

Alternatively, delete the Subscription and the ClusterServiceVersion with the CLI:

oc delete subscription hibernation-operator -n hibernation-operator-system
oc delete csv -n hibernation-operator-system \
  -l operators.coreos.com/hibernation-operator.hibernation-operator-system

OLM does not remove the CRDs either.

docs.title: 3. Remove the CRDs and the namespace
docs.text:
Once no custom resources remain, the CRDs and the operator namespace can be removed:

kubectl delete crd \
  resourcesupervisors.hibernation.stakater.com \
  clusterresourcesupervisors.hibernation.stakater.com
kubectl delete namespace hibernation-operator-system

docs.title: Recovering from an incorrect order
docs.text:
If the operator was removed while supervisors still existed, their deletion remains pending. The simplest recovery is to reinstall the operator, which then processes the pending deletions and restores the workloads.

If reinstalling is not possible, record the replica counts from status.sleepingNamespaces of each pending resource, scale the workloads back manually, and then remove the finalizer that keeps the resource pending:

kubectl patch clusterresourcesupervisor <name> --type merge \
  -p '{"metadata":{"finalizers":null}}'

Removing the finalizer without first restoring the workloads discards the only record of their replica counts.

docs.title: On Kubernetes
docs.text: This page describes how to install the Hibernation Operator on Kubernetes with Helm. To remove the operator, refer to Uninstalling.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A Kubernetes cluster, version 1.24 or later
  • The Helm CLI
  • kubectl
  • cert-manager, installed in the cluster

The chart always deploys the validating admission webhook, and it issues the webhook and metrics certificates through a cert-manager Issuer. cert-manager is therefore required, and the chart provides no option to disable it.

docs.title: Install the operator
docs.text:
The chart is published as an OCI artifact in the Stakater package registry. Install it into the hibernation-operator-system namespace:

helm install hibernation-operator \
  oci://ghcr.io/stakater/public/charts/hibernation-operator \
  --namespace hibernation-operator-system \
  --create-namespace

For production clusters, pin the chart to a specific version by adding --version <chart-version>.

The release creates:

  • The hibernation-operator-controller-manager deployment, which runs the ResourceSupervisor and ClusterResourceSupervisor controllers
  • The hibernation-operator-webhook deployment, which serves the validating admission webhook
  • The CRDs, RBAC resources, services and cert-manager certificates

For the available chart values, refer to Configuration.

docs.title: Verify the installation
docs.text:
kubectl get pods -n hibernation-operator-system --watch

Once both pods report Running, hibernation schedules can be created:

  • Hibernate Workloads in a Single Namespace
  • Hibernate Workloads Across Multiple Namespaces

The ArgoCD integration requires no installation option. It is enabled per resource through spec.argocd on a ClusterResourceSupervisor; refer to ArgoCD Integration.

docs.title: On OpenShift
docs.text:
The Hibernation Operator is a Red Hat Certified Operator available on the Red Hat Marketplace and OperatorHub in OpenShift.

This page describes how to install the Hibernation Operator on OpenShift, either through the OperatorHub UI or declaratively with the CLI. To remove the operator, refer to Uninstalling.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• An OpenShift cluster (v4.10 or higher recommended)

cert-manager is not required on OpenShift. OLM manages the certificate for the validating admission webhook itself.

docs.title: Installing via OperatorHub UI
docs.text:
1. In the OpenShift Console, navigate to Operators → OperatorHub from the left sidebar.
  2. Search for Hibernation Operator and click on the tile.
  3. Click the Install button.
  1. Configure the installation:
  2. Update channel: release-0.1
  3. Installed Namespace: Select hibernation-operator-system (create if it doesn’t exist)
  4. Update approval:
    • Automatic for development
    • Manual for production (allows review of upgrades)

Click Install.

  1. Wait for the operator to install. You’ll see a status of Installed operator: Ready for use when ready.
  2. Once installed, the Hibernation Operator is ready to manage hibernation policies across your cluster.

Note: The operator is installed in the hibernation-operator-system namespace by default.

docs.title: Installing via CLI or GitOps
docs.text: Use this method for automation, CI/CD pipelines, or GitOps workflows (e.g., with ArgoCD).

docs.title: Step 1: Create the Operator Namespace
docs.text: oc create namespace hibernation-operator-system

docs.title: Step 2: Create an OperatorGroup
docs.text:
oc create -f - << EOF
apiVersion: operators.coreos.com/v1
kind: OperatorGroup
metadata:
  name: hibernation-operator
  namespace: hibernation-operator-system
spec: {}
EOF

docs.title: Step 3: Create a Subscription
docs.text:
oc create -f - << EOF
apiVersion: operators.coreos.com/v1alpha1
kind: Subscription
metadata:
  name: hibernation-operator
  namespace: hibernation-operator-system
spec:
  channel: release-0.1
  installPlanApproval: Automatic
  name: hibernation-operator
  source: certified-operators
  sourceNamespace: openshift-marketplace
  # Optional: pin to a specific version
  # startingCSV: hibernation-operator.v0.1.102
EOF

GitOps Tip: Commit these YAMLs to your GitOps repo to manage the operator declaratively.

docs.title: Step 4: Verify Installation
docs.text:
In the OpenShift Console:

  • Go to Operators → Installed Operators
  • Select the hibernation-operator-system project
  • Confirm the Hibernation Operator status is Succeeded

Or via CLI:

oc get csv -n hibernation-operator-system
oc get pods -n hibernation-operator-system

Wait until the hibernation-operator-controller-manager and hibernation-operator-webhook pods are Running.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• It integrates natively with OpenShift workloads (Deployments, StatefulSets) and ArgoCD (if installed).
  • For production, use Manual approval and test upgrades in a staging cluster first.
  • Full CRD documentation:
    • ClusterResourceSupervisor
    • ResourceSupervisor
    • API Reference — generated field reference

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The Hibernation Operator can be installed with the Operator Lifecycle Manager (OLM) or with Helm. Both methods deploy the same controller, admission webhook, CRDs and RBAC resources.

  • Cluster administrator permissions
  • kubectl, or oc on OpenShift
  • The Helm CLI, when installing with Helm
  • cert-manager, when installing with Helm

docs.title: Hibernate Workloads Across Multiple Namespaces
docs.text:
A ClusterResourceSupervisor applies one hibernation schedule to a group of namespaces. It is cluster-scoped, so it suits a platform team parking development or test environments outside working hours, rather than a single team managing its own namespace.

For one namespace owned by the team that hibernates it, use a ResourceSupervisor instead.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The Hibernation Operator is installed in the cluster.
  • You have cluster-admin permissions.

docs.title: Step 1: Choose how to select namespaces
docs.text:
Namespaces come from spec.namespaces, either listed by name, matched by label, or both. The two are combined, so a namespace selected either way is hibernated.

Field Selects spec.namespaces.names A fixed list of namespaces you name explicitly spec.namespaces.labelSelector Every namespace matching the labels, re-evaluated as namespaces come and go

Warning

A ClusterResourceSupervisor with no spec.namespaces hibernates nothing. This matters most when using the ArgoCD integration described below, which does not select namespaces on its own.

An empty labelSelector: {} also matches nothing. To select broadly, use a label every target namespace carries rather than an empty selector.

docs.title: Step 2: Define the ClusterResourceSupervisor
docs.text:
Selecting by label, so namespaces labelled env=dev are picked up automatically as they are created:

apiVersion: hibernation.stakater.com/v1beta1
kind: ClusterResourceSupervisor
metadata:
  name: dev-environments-hibernation
spec:
  namespaces:
    labelSelector:
      matchLabels:
        env: dev
  schedule:
    sleepSchedule: "0 18 * * 1-5"   # Weekdays at 18:00 UTC
    wakeSchedule: "0 8 * * 1-5"     # Weekdays at 08:00 UTC

Selecting a fixed set by name:

apiVersion: hibernation.stakater.com/v1beta1
kind: ClusterResourceSupervisor
metadata:
  name: specific-namespaces-hibernation
spec:
  namespaces:
    names:
      - team-a-staging
      - team-b-test
      - demo-env
  schedule:
    sleepSchedule: "0 0 * * 0"      # Sundays at midnight UTC
    wakeSchedule: "0 0 * * 1"       # Mondays at midnight UTC

Schedules use five-field Unix cron syntax in UTC. Omitting wakeSchedule leaves the workloads asleep until the resource is edited or deleted.

docs.title: Step 3: Apply it
docs.text: kubectl apply -f cluster-resource-supervisor.yaml

docs.title: Step 4: Check the status
docs.text:
kubectl get clusterresourcesupervisor dev-environments-hibernation -o yaml
Field Shows status.currentStatus running, sleeping, or error status.watchedNamespaces Namespaces currently being managed status.ignoreNamespaces Selected namespaces that were filtered out status.sleepingNamespaces Per-namespace detail of the scaled-down workloads status.nextReconcileTime Next scheduled sleep or wake status.conditions Ready, False with the reason when a sleep or wake fails. See Troubleshooting

If a namespace you expected is missing from watchedNamespaces, check ignoreNamespaces. Namespaces annotated hibernation.stakater.com/exclude: "true", and the operator's own namespace, are always filtered out.

docs.title: Keeping ArgoCD from waking workloads
docs.text:
When applications are managed by ArgoCD, scaling them to zero puts them out of sync with Git, and ArgoCD will scale them back up. The spec.argocd field addresses this by writing a deny sync window onto the named AppProjects, matching the sleep schedule and its computed duration.

apiVersion: hibernation.stakater.com/v1beta1
kind: ClusterResourceSupervisor
metadata:
  name: argocd-frontend-hibernation
spec:
  namespaces:
    labelSelector:
      matchLabels:
        team: frontend
  argocd:
    namespace: argocd          # Namespace where the AppProjects live
    appProjects:
      - frontend-team
      - mobile-apps
  schedule:
    sleepSchedule: "0 22 * * *"
    wakeSchedule: "0 6 * * *"

Warning

spec.argocd does not select namespaces. It only suppresses ArgoCD syncing for the AppProjects you name, and the namespaces to hibernate still come entirely from spec.namespaces. The example above hibernates the team=frontend namespaces; without that namespaces block it would hibernate nothing while still writing sync windows.

Two further points before enabling this:

  • The operator replaces spec.syncWindows on each named AppProject rather than appending to it. Any sync windows you maintain there by other means are overwritten.
  • The integration requires the ArgoCD AppProject CRD to be present, and needs no installation option. If the CRD is absent, the operator logs the fact and continues hibernating. Refer to ArgoCD Integration.

docs.title: Hibernate Workloads in a Single Namespace
Hibernate Workloads in a Single Namespace
docs.text:
A ResourceSupervisor scales the Deployments and StatefulSets in its own namespace down to zero on a schedule, and back to their original replica counts when the wake schedule fires. It is namespace-scoped, so a team that owns a namespace can set this up without cluster-wide permissions.

To cover several namespaces at once, use a ClusterResourceSupervisor instead.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The Hibernation Operator is installed in the cluster.
  • You have edit permissions in the namespace you want to hibernate.

docs.title: Step 1: Define the ResourceSupervisor
docs.text:
Create resource-supervisor.yaml. The metadata.namespace is the namespace that will be hibernated, since the resource only acts on its own namespace.

apiVersion: hibernation.stakater.com/v1beta1
kind: ResourceSupervisor
metadata:
  name: my-namespace-hibernation
  namespace: my-app-staging
spec:
  schedule:
    sleepSchedule: "0 20 * * *"   # Sleep daily at 20:00 UTC
    wakeSchedule: "0 8 * * *"     # Wake daily at 08:00 UTC

Note

Both schedules use standard five-field Unix cron syntax (minute hour day month weekday) and are evaluated in UTC, not the cluster's local timezone. crontab.guru is useful for checking an expression before applying it.

Omitting wakeSchedule puts the workloads to sleep and leaves them there until you edit or delete the resource. That is a deliberate option for environments you want parked indefinitely, but it is easy to do by accident.

docs.title: Step 2: Apply it
docs.text: kubectl apply -f resource-supervisor.yaml

docs.title: Step 3: Check the status
docs.text:
kubectl get resourcesupervisor my-namespace-hibernation -n my-app-staging -o yaml

Two fields tell you where things stand:

  • status.currentStatus is running, sleeping, or error.
  • status.nextReconcileTime is the next time the operator will sleep or wake the workloads.
  • The Ready condition in status.conditions is True after a successful sleep or wake, and False with the reason when one fails. See Troubleshooting.

docs.title: What gets hibernated
docs.text:
Only Deployments and StatefulSets in the same namespace are touched. Other workload types, and resources in any other namespace, are left alone. Workloads already sitting at zero replicas are skipped rather than recorded as sleeping.

Before scaling a workload down, the operator records its replica count in the supervisor's status.sleepingNamespaces. Waking restores exactly that count and touches nothing it did not sleep, so you can always see what a sleeping workload will return to:

kubectl get resourcesupervisor my-namespace-hibernation -n my-app-staging \
  -o jsonpath='{range .status.sleepingNamespaces[*].sleepingApplications[*]}{.kind}/{.name}: {.replicas}{"\n"}{end}'

Deleting the ResourceSupervisor wakes its workloads first. The resource is retained until the restore succeeds, so removing the supervisor is a safe way to cancel hibernation rather than a way to strand workloads at zero.

A namespace annotated with hibernation.stakater.com/exclude: "true" is skipped, even if a ResourceSupervisor exists in it.

docs.title: Hibernate a Tenant
docs.text:
This guide describes how to hibernate every namespace that belongs to a Multi-Tenant Operator tenant by using a ClusterResourceSupervisor.

Note

The spec.hibernation field was removed from the Tenant resource in MTO 1.7. Tenant hibernation is configured with a ClusterResourceSupervisor that selects the tenant's namespaces by label.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The Hibernation Operator is installed in the cluster. Refer to Installation.
  • Permission to create ClusterResourceSupervisor resources, which are cluster scoped.

docs.title: Hibernate all namespaces of a tenant
docs.text:
MTO applies the label stakater.com/tenant: <tenant-name> to every namespace it manages for a tenant. A ClusterResourceSupervisor can select those namespaces with a single label selector:

apiVersion: hibernation.stakater.com/v1beta1
kind: ClusterResourceSupervisor
metadata:
  name: sigma-hibernation
spec:
  schedule:
    sleepSchedule: "0 20 * * 1-5"   # 20:00 UTC, Monday to Friday
    wakeSchedule: "0 8 * * 1-5"     # 08:00 UTC, Monday to Friday
  namespaces:
    labelSelector:
      matchLabels:
        stakater.com/tenant: sigma

At 20:00 UTC on each weekday, every Deployment and StatefulSet in the namespaces of the sigma tenant is scaled to zero, and its replica count is recorded in the resource status. At 08:00 UTC, each workload is restored to its recorded count. Namespaces created for the tenant later are included at the next scheduled sleep or wake.

docs.title: Keep a namespace of the tenant running
docs.text:
To exclude one of the tenant's namespaces, annotate it rather than changing the selector:

kubectl annotate namespace sigma-prod hibernation.stakater.com/exclude=true

The exclusion applies to every supervisor, whether it was created for a tenant or not. Excluded namespaces are listed in status.ignoreNamespaces.

docs.title: Tenants deployed with ArgoCD
docs.text:
If the tenant's workloads are deployed by ArgoCD, ArgoCD synchronises them back to their declared replica count after they are hibernated. To prevent this, name the tenant's AppProjects under spec.argocd:

apiVersion: hibernation.stakater.com/v1beta1
kind: ClusterResourceSupervisor
metadata:
  name: sigma-hibernation
spec:
  schedule:
    sleepSchedule: "0 20 * * 1-5"
    wakeSchedule: "0 8 * * 1-5"
  namespaces:
    labelSelector:
      matchLabels:
        stakater.com/tenant: sigma
  argocd:
    namespace: openshift-gitops
    appProjects:
      - sigma

The operator applies a deny sync window to the sigma AppProject for the duration of the sleep period. spec.argocd does not select namespaces; the namespaces are still selected by spec.namespaces. Refer to ArgoCD Integration before enabling it.

docs.title: Verify the status
docs.text:
While the tenant is hibernated, the status of the resource lists each workload and the replica count it will be restored to:

status:
  currentStatus: sleeping
  nextReconcileTime: "2026-06-11T08:00:00Z"
  watchedNamespaces:
    - sigma-dev
    - sigma-staging
  sleepingNamespaces:
    - Namespace: sigma-dev
      sleepingApplications:
        - kind: Deployment
          name: web
          replicas: 3
    - Namespace: sigma-staging
      sleepingApplications:
        - kind: StatefulSet
          name: database
          replicas: 1

docs.title: ArgoCD Integration
docs.text:
When workloads are managed by ArgoCD, hibernation and GitOps pull in opposite directions. Scaling a Deployment to zero is drift from the desired state in Git, so ArgoCD syncs it back up and the workloads never stay asleep.

The Hibernation Operator resolves this by writing a deny sync window onto the ArgoCD AppProjects you name, covering the sleep period. ArgoCD then leaves those applications alone while they are hibernated, and resumes normal syncing afterwards.

Warning

spec.argocd does not choose which namespaces to hibernate. It only suppresses ArgoCD syncing. The namespaces still come entirely from spec.namespaces, and a ClusterResourceSupervisor with an argocd block but no namespaces block writes sync windows while hibernating nothing.

The integration is optional and is enabled per resource by setting spec.argocd on a ClusterResourceSupervisor. No installation option is required.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
When a ClusterResourceSupervisor sets spec.argocd, the operator:

  1. Looks up each named AppProject in the namespace given by spec.argocd.namespace.
  2. Computes the sleep duration from sleepSchedule and wakeSchedule.
  3. Sets a single deny sync window on the AppProject, scheduled to match the sleep time and lasting that duration, with manual sync still permitted.

Hibernation of the workloads themselves proceeds independently, driven by spec.namespaces as usual.

Warning

The operator replaces spec.syncWindows on each named AppProject rather than appending to it. Sync windows you maintain there by other means are overwritten. If you rely on existing sync windows, do not point the operator at that AppProject.

If the ArgoCD AppProject CRD is not present in the cluster, the operator logs that and continues hibernating without touching ArgoCD.

docs.title: Using it
docs.text:
Select the namespaces to hibernate as normal, and list the AppProjects whose syncing should be suppressed while they sleep:

apiVersion: hibernation.stakater.com/v1beta1
kind: ClusterResourceSupervisor
metadata:
  name: argocd-hibernation-policy
spec:
  namespaces:
    labelSelector:
      matchLabels:
        env: dev
  argocd:
    namespace: argocd          # Namespace where the AppProjects live
    appProjects:
      - frontend-team
      - mobile-apps
  schedule:
    sleepSchedule: "0 18 * * 1-5"   # Sleep weekdays at 18:00 UTC
    wakeSchedule: "0 8 * * 1-5"     # Wake weekdays at 08:00 UTC

Apply it:

kubectl apply -f cluster-resource-supervisor-argocd.yaml

docs.title: Verifying
docs.text:
Check which namespaces the policy actually manages. These come from spec.namespaces, not from the AppProjects:

kubectl get clusterresourcesupervisor argocd-hibernation-policy -o jsonpath='{.status.watchedNamespaces}'

Then confirm the sync window landed on the AppProject:

kubectl get appproject frontend-team -n argocd -o jsonpath='{.spec.syncWindows}'

You should see a single entry with kind: deny and a schedule matching your sleepSchedule.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
ArgoCD must be installed, and the operator's ServiceAccount needs to read and modify AppProjects in the ArgoCD namespace, since writing the sync window is a patch rather than a read:

- apiGroups: ["argoproj.io"]
  resources: ["appprojects"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "update", "patch"]

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Check No sync window appears on the AppProject The name in appProjects matches the AppProject resource name exactly, and spec.argocd.namespace is the namespace it lives in. Both are case-sensitive. Sync window exists but nothing hibernates spec.namespaces is set. The argocd block alone selects no namespaces. Namespace missing from status.watchedNamespaces status.ignoreNamespaces, which lists namespaces filtered out by the hibernation.stakater.com/exclude annotation or because they are the operator's own namespace. Workloads wake up during the sleep window The sync window was overwritten, or the application belongs to an AppProject not listed in spec.argocd.appProjects. Permission errors in the operator log The ServiceAccount has update and patch on appprojects.argoproj.io, not only read verbs.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text: The operator is driven by two custom resources that share the same schedule format and the same status format. They differ only in who creates them and in how many namespaces they govern.

docs.title: Sleep and wake on a cron schedule
docs.text:
Most non-production environments are idle at night and at weekends, and hibernation removes those hours from the cost of running them. The spec.schedule field accepts a sleepSchedule and a wakeSchedule, each expressed as a standard five-field cron expression and evaluated in UTC. Both fields are optional, and the combination that is set determines the behaviour:

sleepSchedule wakeSchedule Behaviour Set Set Workloads sleep at each sleep time and wake at each wake time Set Empty Workloads sleep at the next sleep time and remain asleep Empty Empty Workloads sleep immediately and remain asleep until the schedule is changed or the resource is deleted Empty Set Rejected by the admission webhook, as there is no sleep period to apply

The admission webhook also rejects cron expressions that cannot be parsed, and sleep and wake schedules that are identical.

For further details, refer to ResourceSupervisor and ClusterResourceSupervisor.

docs.title: Restore every workload to its previous replica count
docs.text:
A hibernated environment must come back exactly as it was. Before any workload is scaled down, the operator records its replica count in status.sleepingNamespaces on the resource responsible for hibernating it. Workloads are restored exclusively from this record, which ensures that:

  • Each workload is restored to its own replica count rather than to a default value.
  • Workloads that the operator did not hibernate are never modified when it restores others.
  • Workloads already scaled to zero are skipped, so that their recorded count is never overwritten with zero.
  • The record is stored in the Kubernetes API and therefore persists across operator restarts.

When a supervisor is deleted, its workloads are restored before the deletion completes. If a restoration fails, the resource is retained until it succeeds.

Hibernation applies to Deployments and StatefulSets only. PersistentVolumeClaims, and the storage costs associated with them, are not affected.

docs.title: Hibernate one namespace or many
docs.text:
Hibernation can be decided by the team that owns a namespace or by the platform team that runs the cluster, and each has its own resource:

ResourceSupervisor ClusterResourceSupervisor Scope Namespace Cluster Governs The namespace in which it is created Every namespace it selects Created by Any user permitted to create it in that namespace A cluster administrator Namespace targeting Not applicable Namespace names and label selectors ArgoCD sync windows Not supported Supported

The admission webhook prevents two ClusterResourceSupervisor resources from selecting the same namespace. It does not, however, prevent a ClusterResourceSupervisor and a ResourceSupervisor from governing the same namespace, so such overlaps must be avoided by convention.

docs.title: Select namespaces by name or label
docs.text:
A platform team decides which environments are hibernated by selecting their namespaces. A ClusterResourceSupervisor combines two lists defined under spec.namespaces:

  • names: namespaces specified explicitly by name.
  • labelSelector: a standard Kubernetes label selector using matchLabels and matchExpressions. Namespaces created later with matching labels are included at the next scheduled sleep or wake.

A label selector that defines neither matchLabels nor matchExpressions selects no namespaces, rather than all of them.

When a namespace is removed from the scope of a supervisor, any workloads the supervisor had hibernated in that namespace are restored.

For further details, refer to Hibernate Workloads Across Multiple Namespaces.

docs.title: Exclude namespaces from hibernation
docs.text:
Some namespaces must never be hibernated, whatever schedule selects them. A namespace carrying the following annotation is never hibernated by a supervisor of either kind:

metadata:
  annotations:
    hibernation.stakater.com/exclude: "true"

An exclusion takes precedence over every schedule. Any workloads that a supervisor had already hibernated in the namespace are restored at its next scheduled sleep or wake. The namespace in which the operator runs is always excluded. Excluded namespaces are listed in status.ignoreNamespaces, which explains why a schedule may have had no effect.

docs.title: Keep ArgoCD from undoing hibernation
docs.text:
ArgoCD treats a workload scaled to zero as drift from the desired state in Git and synchronises it back to its declared replica count. When spec.argocd is set on a ClusterResourceSupervisor, the operator applies a deny sync window to each specified AppProject. The window opens at the sleep time and remains in effect until the wake time. Manual synchronisation remains permitted.

The spec.argocd field does not determine which namespaces are hibernated; these are always selected through spec.namespaces. Because the sync window is derived from sleepSchedule, no window is applied when that field is empty.

Warning

The operator replaces the existing spec.syncWindows of each AppProject with its own window, and removes all sync windows when the supervisor is deleted. It should therefore not be used with AppProjects that define sync windows of their own.

Warning

The operator's ClusterRole does not include permissions on appprojects in the argoproj.io API group. Grant get and patch on this resource to the operator's service account before using spec.argocd.

For further details, refer to ArgoCD Integration.

docs.title: Track hibernation state in the resource status
docs.text:
The status of each resource shows what is currently hibernated and when that will change. Both resources report the same fields:

Field Description currentStatus The current state: sleeping, running or error nextReconcileTime The time at which the next sleep or wake is due watchedNamespaces The namespaces the supervisor is permitted to hibernate ignoreNamespaces The namespaces that were selected but cannot be hibernated, because they are excluded or no longer exist sleepingNamespaces Each hibernated workload, with its kind, its recorded replica count and, after a failed wake, an errorMessage conditions A Ready condition stating whether the last sleep or wake succeeded and, if not, the reason

If a sleep or wake fails, currentStatus is set to error, the Ready condition records the reason, such as SleepFailed, WakeFailed or InvalidSleepSchedule, and the operation is retried. The same failures are also reported as Kubernetes events on the resource. For further details, refer to Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Use Cases
docs.text: The Hibernation Operator is intended for clusters that run environments continuously, even though those environments are only used for part of the day. The scenarios below describe the situations for which it was designed.

docs.title: Development and test platforms
docs.text:
Scenario: A platform team operates a shared cluster for many development teams. Each team maintains dev, test and staging namespaces, all of which continue to run overnight and at weekends while no one is using them.

Approach: A single ClusterResourceSupervisor selects every non-production namespace by label and hibernates those namespaces outside working hours:

apiVersion: hibernation.stakater.com/v1beta1
kind: ClusterResourceSupervisor
metadata:
  name: non-production-office-hours
spec:
  schedule:
    sleepSchedule: "0 19 * * 1-5"
    wakeSchedule: "0 7 * * 1-5"
  namespaces:
    labelSelector:
      matchExpressions:
        - key: env
          operator: In
          values: [dev, test, staging]

Newly created namespaces with a matching label are included without any change to the supervisor. A namespace that must remain available, for example during a demonstration or a load test, is annotated with hibernation.stakater.com/exclude: "true" rather than being removed from the selector.

docs.title: Team self-service
docs.text:
Scenario: A product team owns the payments-staging namespace and is best placed to determine its own working hours. The team should be able to reduce costs without raising a request with the platform team or holding cluster-level permissions.

Approach: The team creates a ResourceSupervisor in its own namespace. Because the resource can only affect the namespace in which it is created, permission to create it can safely be granted to namespace owners, and each team can define its own schedule. For further details, refer to Hibernate Workloads in a Single Namespace.

docs.title: GitOps-managed environments
docs.text:
Scenario: The environments are deployed by ArgoCD. A workload scaled to zero is treated as drift from Git, so ArgoCD synchronises it back to its declared replica count and hibernation does not take effect.

Approach: A ClusterResourceSupervisor that specifies the relevant AppProjects under spec.argocd applies a deny sync window to them for the duration of the sleep period, so that ArgoCD does not restore the hibernated workloads before the wake time. The namespaces to be hibernated are still selected under spec.namespaces. For further details, refer to ArgoCD Integration.

docs.title: Holiday and shutdown periods
docs.text:
Scenario: During an organisation-wide closure, non-critical environments should remain unavailable for the entire period and be restored only when a deliberate decision is made to do so.

Approach: A ClusterResourceSupervisor with an empty schedule hibernates the selected namespaces immediately and keeps them hibernated. Deleting the supervisor at the end of the period restores every workload to its recorded replica count.

apiVersion: hibernation.stakater.com/v1beta1
kind: ClusterResourceSupervisor
metadata:
  name: year-end-shutdown
spec:
  schedule: {}
  namespaces:
    labelSelector:
      matchLabels:
        criticality: low

docs.title: Demonstration and training environments
docs.text:
Scenario: Environments used for customer demonstrations or training are only required during business hours, and many copies of them may exist at any time.

Approach: A ResourceSupervisor is included in the environment template, so every copy is provisioned with a hibernation schedule already in place and no manual intervention is required.

docs.title: Multi-tenant clusters
docs.text:
Scenario: A cluster hosts many tenants, and the non-production environments of lower-tier tenants are not required to run overnight.

Approach: A ClusterResourceSupervisor selects namespaces by a tenant or tier label, such as tier: basic, while namespaces belonging to other tenants continue to run. When Multi-Tenant Operator is in use, every tenant namespace already carries the stakater.com/tenant: <tenant-name> label, so a single selector can cover an entire tenant.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
The operator is not the appropriate tool in the following situations:

  • Ephemeral environments that should be removed: Hibernation retains the namespace, its configuration and its volumes. Preview environments that are no longer needed should be deleted instead.
  • Storage costs: Only Deployments and StatefulSets are scaled. PersistentVolumeClaims are not affected.
  • Other workload kinds: DaemonSets, Jobs, CronJobs and custom workload resources are not hibernated.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
This page documents the configuration surface of the Hibernation Operator: the Helm chart values you set at install time, the environment variables that toggle controllers and webhooks, and the manager command-line flags that control the metrics, health, and webhook endpoints.

For the full installation flow, see Installation › Kubernetes.

docs.title: Helm values
docs.text:
The operator is installed from the OCI chart oci://ghcr.io/stakater/public/charts/hibernation-operator. The table below lists the values most commonly tuned. Inspect the full set with:

helm show values oci://ghcr.io/stakater/public/charts/hibernation-operator
Value Default Description controllerManager.controllerManager.env.enableRsController "true" Enable the ResourceSupervisor controller. controllerManager.controllerManager.env.enableCrsController "true" Enable the cluster-scoped ClusterResourceSupervisor controller. controllerManager.controllerManager.env.enableWebhooks "false" Enable validating webhooks on the controller deployment. controllerManager.controllerManager.env.leaderElectionId hibernation-operator-election-id Leader-election lock identifier. controllerManager.controllerManager.image.repository ghcr.io/stakater/public/hibernation-operator Operator image repository. controllerManager.controllerManager.image.tag the release tag, for example v0.1.104 Operator image tag. controllerManager.controllerManager.resources requests 10m/64Mi, limits 500m/128Mi Manager container resource requests/limits. controllerManager.replicas 1 Number of manager replicas. webhook.manager.env.enableWebhooks "true" Enable webhooks on the dedicated webhook deployment. webhook.manager.resources requests 100m/20Mi, limits 2/2Gi Webhook container resource requests/limits. webhook.replicas 1 Number of webhook deployment replicas. imagePullSecrets [] Image pull secrets for private registries. kubernetesClusterDomain cluster.local Cluster DNS domain (used for in-cluster service URLs).

For example, to disable the ResourceSupervisor controller at install time:

helm install hibernation-operator \
  oci://ghcr.io/stakater/public/charts/hibernation-operator \
  --namespace hibernation-operator-system --create-namespace \
  --set controllerManager.controllerManager.env.enableRsController="false"

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
These are consumed by the operator process directly (the Helm chart sets them on the deployment). Flag variables are enabled only when set to the exact string "true".

Variable Default Description ENABLE_RS_CONTROLLER unset (off) Enable the ResourceSupervisor controller. ENABLE_CRS_CONTROLLER unset (off) Enable the ClusterResourceSupervisor controller. ENABLE_WEBHOOKS unset (off) Enable the validating webhooks. OPERATOR_NAME_PREFIX hibernation-operator Name prefix used for operator-owned resources. OPERATOR_NAMESPACE auto-detected in-cluster, falling back to hibernation-operator-system Namespace the operator runs in. Workloads in this namespace are never hibernated. LEADER_ELECTION_ID unset Identifier for the leader-election lock. When unset, leader election is disabled even if --leader-elect is passed.

docs.title: Manager flags
docs.text:
Command-line flags accepted by the manager binary (set via the deployment's container args).

Flag Default Description --metrics-bind-address 0 (disabled) Address the metrics endpoint binds to, or 0 to disable it. The Helm chart and the OLM bundle set :6443. --metrics-tls-cert-dir "" Directory containing tls.crt and tls.key. When set, metrics are served over https; otherwise over http. --metrics-secure true Accepted but has no effect. Use --metrics-tls-cert-dir to enable https. --health-probe-bind-address :8081 Address for liveness/readiness probes. --pprof-bind-address 0 (disabled) Address the pprof profiling endpoint binds to, 0 to disable. Prefer a local address such as 127.0.0.1:6060 with a port forward, anything else publishes profiling data to the cluster network. -zap-devel false Switch logs to console output at Debug level for a local run. The default is production mode, JSON at Info with stack traces at Error. --leader-elect false Enable leader election for high-availability deployments. --enable-http2 false Enable HTTP/2 for the metrics and webhook servers. Disabled by default to mitigate HTTP/2 CVEs. --webhook-cert-path "" Directory containing the webhook certificate. --webhook-cert-name tls.crt Webhook certificate file name. --webhook-cert-key tls.key Webhook key file name. --metrics-cert-path "" Directory containing the metrics server certificate. --metrics-cert-name tls.crt Metrics certificate file name. --metrics-cert-key tls.key Metrics key file name.

The standard -zap-log-level, -zap-encoder and -zap-stacktrace-level flags are accepted as well.

See Metrics for how the metrics endpoint is exposed, and Webhooks for webhook certificate management.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text: The Hibernation Operator exposes Prometheus metrics through the controller-runtime metrics server.

docs.title: Metrics endpoint
docs.text:
The metrics server is controlled by the --metrics-bind-address flag. The binary disables it by default (0), but both the Helm chart and the OLM bundle start the controller manager with --metrics-bind-address=:6443, so an installed operator serves metrics on port 6443 at the path /metrics.

The server uses TLS only when --metrics-tls-cert-dir points to a directory containing tls.crt and tls.key. Neither installation method sets this flag, so the endpoint is served over plain http by default. The --metrics-secure flag is accepted but has no effect.

Requests pass through the controller-runtime authentication and authorization filter, which validates the caller's bearer token against the Kubernetes API. The scraping principal therefore needs the hibernation-operator-metrics-reader ClusterRole. Refer to RBAC.

The webhook deployment does not serve metrics.

docs.title: Scraping
docs.text: Neither installation method ships a ServiceMonitor. To scrape the operator with the Prometheus Operator, create a Service that targets port 6443 of the hibernation-operator-controller-manager pods, and a ServiceMonitor that selects it and authenticates with a token bound to the metrics reader role.

docs.title: Available metrics
docs.text:
The operator exports the standard controller-runtime metrics and defines no hibernation-specific metrics. These include:

  • controller_runtime_reconcile_total: reconciles per controller and result
  • controller_runtime_reconcile_errors_total: reconcile errors per controller
  • controller_runtime_reconcile_time_seconds: reconcile latency histogram
  • workqueue_*: depth, additions, latency and retries of the controller work queues
  • rest_client_*: Kubernetes API client request metrics

These metrics describe the reconcile health, error rates and API client behaviour of both the ResourceSupervisor and ClusterResourceSupervisor controllers.

docs.title: RBAC
docs.text: The Hibernation Operator ships with a least-privilege set of RBAC roles: the permissions the controller itself needs to operate, and a set of user-facing roles you can bind to your own users and groups for self-service access to the custom resources.

docs.title: Operator (manager) permissions
docs.text:
The operator's hibernation-operator-manager-role ClusterRole grants only what is required to watch the custom resources and scale workloads:

API group Resources Verbs "" (core) events create, patch "" (core) namespaces get, list, watch apiextensions.k8s.io customresourcedefinitions get, list, watch apps deployments, statefulsets get, list, patch, update, watch hibernation.stakater.com clusterresourcesupervisors, resourcesupervisors create, delete, get, list, patch, update, watch hibernation.stakater.com clusterresourcesupervisors/status, resourcesupervisors/status get, patch, update hibernation.stakater.com clusterresourcesupervisors/finalizers, resourcesupervisors/finalizers update

The operator has read-only access to namespaces and CRDs. Apart from its own custom resources and the events it records on them, it modifies only Deployments and StatefulSets, to scale them. See the Security Model for how this supports safe operation.

docs.title: User-facing roles
docs.text:
For each custom resource the chart provides admin, editor and viewer ClusterRoles, named hibernation-operator-<resource>-<role>-role, for binding to users and groups:

Role ResourceSupervisor ClusterResourceSupervisor admin full access (*) to the resource; get on status full access (*) to the resource; get on status editor create, delete, get, list, patch, update, watch; get on status create, delete, get, list, patch, update, watch; get on status viewer get, list, watch get, list, watch

Bind one of these to a user or group, for example:

kubectl create rolebinding alice-rs-editor \
  --clusterrole=hibernation-operator-resourcesupervisor-editor-role \
  --user=alice \
  --namespace=my-app-staging

docs.title: Leader election and metrics roles
docs.text:
• Leader election: a Role granting access to coordination.k8s.io leases and events, used only when --leader-elect is enabled.
  • Metrics access: a metrics-reader role (read the /metrics endpoint) and a metrics-auth role used by the authentication/authorization filter that protects the metrics endpoint. See Metrics.

docs.title: Security Model
docs.text: The Hibernation Operator is designed to run safely in shared and multi-tenant clusters. Its security model rests on four pillars: hardened workloads, least-privilege RBAC, namespace-level safety controls, and secured transport.

docs.title: Pod and container hardening
docs.text:
The controller manager deployment meets the Kubernetes restricted Pod Security Standard:

  • Pod: runAsNonRoot: true, seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault
  • Container: allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, all Linux capabilities dropped (capabilities.drop: ["ALL"])

The webhook deployment sets runAsNonRoot: true and allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, but it sets no seccompProfile and does not drop capabilities, so it meets the baseline standard rather than the restricted one.

Both deployments set resource requests and limits.

docs.title: Least-privilege RBAC
docs.text:
Both deployments run under the dedicated hibernation-operator-controller-manager ServiceAccount, bound to a tightly scoped ClusterRole:

  • Read-only on namespaces and customresourcedefinitions.
  • Write access limited to Deployments and StatefulSets (for scaling), the operator's own custom resources, and events.
  • status and finalizers permissions are separated from the main resource rules.

No cluster-admin or wildcard permissions are granted. See RBAC for the complete permission set.

docs.title: Namespace exclusion safety
docs.text:
Workloads can be protected from hibernation regardless of any matching supervisor:

  • A namespace annotated with hibernation.stakater.com/exclude: "true" is always ignored, and the operator never scales workloads in it.
  • The operator's own namespace is automatically excluded.

This lets platform teams carve out critical namespaces (or let application teams opt out of cluster-wide policies) safely. The operator only ever modifies Deployments and StatefulSets it explicitly targets; all other resources are left untouched.

docs.title: Transport security
docs.text:
• Webhooks are served over TLS. The certificate is issued by cert-manager for Helm installations, by OLM on OpenShift, or supplied through flags. See Webhooks.
  • Metrics require a bearer token authorized through the Kubernetes API, but are served over plain http unless --metrics-tls-cert-dir is set. See Metrics.
  • HTTP/2 is disabled by default (--enable-http2=false) to mitigate known HTTP/2 denial-of-service vulnerabilities (e.g. the "Rapid Reset" class of CVEs). Enable it only if you understand the risk.
  • No NetworkPolicy is shipped. To restrict access to the metrics endpoint, create one that limits ingress on port 6443 to your Prometheus instance.

docs.title: Webhooks
docs.text: The Hibernation Operator provides validating admission webhooks for both custom resources. They reject invalid resources at admission time — before they are persisted — primarily to catch malformed cron schedules and conflicting namespace targeting.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• Type: validating only (no mutating webhooks).
  • Resources / operations: resourcesupervisors and clusterresourcesupervisors, on CREATE and UPDATE.
  • Failure policy: Fail — if the webhook is unavailable, the request is rejected (sideEffects: None).
  • Enablement: off by default; enabled via the ENABLE_WEBHOOKS environment variable. The Helm chart runs a dedicated webhook deployment with webhooks enabled (see Configuration).
  • Port: the webhook server listens on 9443.

The webhook endpoints are:

  • /validate-hibernation-stakater-com-v1beta1-resourcesupervisor (vresourcesupervisor.kb.io)
  • /validate-hibernation-stakater-com-v1beta1-clusterresourcesupervisor (vclusterresourcesupervisor.kb.io)

docs.title: Schedule validation (both resources)
docs.text:
Cron schedules are parsed using standard cron syntax. The webhook enforces:

  • Empty schedules are allowed — both sleepSchedule and wakeSchedule empty (immediate/permanent sleep use cases) passes validation.
  • Whichever of sleepSchedule and wakeSchedule is set must be a valid cron expression.
  • sleepSchedule and wakeSchedule must not be identical.
  • A wakeSchedule requires a sleepSchedule. A wake only schedule is rejected.
  • Unless both schedules contain a wildcard (*), both must resolve to a time in the future, and the wake time must be after the sleep time.

Schedules are evaluated in UTC.

docs.title: ClusterResourceSupervisor namespace validation
docs.text:
In addition to schedule validation, the ClusterResourceSupervisor webhook enforces namespace uniqueness:

  • No duplicate namespace names within a single resource's spec.namespaces.names.
  • No overlap across resources — a namespace targeted by one ClusterResourceSupervisor cannot be targeted by another. This prevents two cluster supervisors from fighting over the same namespace.

docs.title: Certificates
docs.text:
The webhook server requires TLS. The operator integrates with cert-manager:

  • A self-signed Issuer (selfsigned-issuer) issues a Certificate stored in the secret hibernation-operator-webhook-server-cert.
  • DNS names cover the webhook service (<service>.<namespace>.svc and the .svc.cluster.local variant).

Alternatively, you can supply certificates directly via the --webhook-cert-path, --webhook-cert-name, and --webhook-cert-key flags.

The Helm chart always deploys the webhook, so cert-manager is required for Helm installations. On OpenShift, OLM manages the webhook certificate. See Installation › Kubernetes.
